screens.title: Cloud Security Shared Responsibility Model
screens.narratorSegment: Today we will make the shared responsibility model clear and usable. This model separates what the cloud provider secures from what you, the customer, must secure. The concise rule to remember is: the provider secures the cloud itself — the data centers, network fabric, and service infrastructure — while you secure everything you place into the cloud: your data, applications, identities, and configurations. Understanding this split prevents expensive gaps and common breaches. In practical terms, when you run an EC2 virtual machine or store files in a managed object store, the provider keeps the hardware and service running; you must patch the operating system, set access policies, and encrypt sensitive data. Throughout this lesson you will see concrete examples for IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS, learn common missteps like public buckets and open security groups, and get clear mitigations to apply in enterprise environments. By the end you should be able to explain responsibility boundaries to stakeholders and design controls that close customer-side gaps.

Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Assessments & Skills
Assessments and Practical Tasks

Tasks focus on mapping breaches to responsibility, and proposing defensible customer controls.

Breach Analysis Task

Configuration Review

Vendor Documentation Check
Use the CSP's shared responsibility matrix to verify the boundary for services you use; do not assume default coverage.
Quick Example

screens.title: Security of the Cloud vs Security in the Cloud
screens.narratorSegment: We begin by defining the two central terms you will use constantly: security of the cloud and security in the cloud. Security of the cloud is the provider's duty to secure the infrastructure that runs services: physical data centers, network fabric, hypervisors, and the internal code that implements managed services. Providers maintain physical access controls, redundant networking, and patching at the service layer so you can rely on a hardened foundation. Security in the cloud is everything you are accountable for when using cloud services: your data, applications, operating systems you deploy, configuration of network controls, and identity management. For example, a CSP will protect the servers that host object storage, but you are responsible for the bucket policies and object ACLs that govern who can read your data. A useful misconception check: never assume a provider configures your service endpoints, access rules, or encryption keys for you by default. The takeaway is a working claim: the CSP secures the environment; you secure your usage of it. To practice, name one service you use and list which parts the provider controls and which parts you must harden. That exercise will reveal hidden responsibilities.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Security of the cloud = CSP duties; security in the cloud = customer duties. Never assume configuration-driven controls are provided for you.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Security of vs in the Cloud
Core Concept

Meaning and scope

Security of the cloud: provider duties for infrastructure, facilities, and managed service integrity. Security in the cloud: customer duties for data, code, OS, IAM, and configurations.

Provider examples
  • Physical security, hypervisor patching, managed service availability
  • Underlying network and storage hardware maintenance
Customer examples
  • OS patching, application hardening, access policies
  • Encryption, logging, IAM configuration
Key Takeaway

Treat infrastructure protections as durable provider-provided controls and treat configuration, data, and identity as actively owned by the customer.

Concrete Example
Imagine an object store service. The CSP ensures the service API is available and the storage hardware is secure. If an object becomes public due to your bucket policy, that exposure is a customer-side failure. Fixing it requires policy changes and account-level public access blocks.
Common Misconception
Assuming the CSP will automatically secure service endpoints and default configurations for your tenant is dangerous. Providers secure the platform, not your specific configuration choices.
Check Your Understanding
Pick a managed database you use and list which parts the provider patches and which parts you must secure, such as credentials and schema-level encryption.

screens.title: Customer responsibilities in IaaS
screens.narratorSegment: In an Infrastructure as a Service model you take on the largest share of security duties. The provider secures the physical hosts, virtualization layer, and the network fabric, but you are responsible for everything you install or configure on your virtual machines and services. That responsibility includes patching and hardening the operating system, managing host-based firewalls and anti-malware, securing application code, managing security groups and network ACLs, encrypting data at rest and in transit, and implementing identity and access controls with least privilege. A common breach pattern is an unpatched virtual machine combined with an overly permissive security group allowing SSH from anywhere; both are customer failures that invite compromise. To operationalize IaaS security, use automated patch management, vulnerability scanning, baseline hardening templates, least-privilege IAM roles, and network segmentation. Also maintain logging and alerts so you can detect unauthorized access quickly. Misconception check: do not assume that because the provider manages the network hardware, your virtual network configuration is secure by default. The immediate takeaway is: treat each VM and storage resource as your operational responsibility and bake patching and configuration as repeatable automation.

keyIdea.text: Customer secures OS, apps, network configs, and data. Automate patching and hardening to reduce exposure.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › IaaS Responsibilities
Process Flow

Customer security steps for IaaS

1
Patching and host hardening
Automate OS updates and establish hardened images for new instances.
2
Network controls
Configure security groups and NACLs to restrict inbound access; avoid open SSH from the internet.
3
Data and encryption
Encrypt sensitive data, manage keys, and classify data to apply appropriate controls.
4
Identity and access
Use IAM, roles, MFA, and least privilege for users and services interacting with your instances.
Example Risk
An EC2 instance with an outdated OS and SSH allowed from 0.0.0.0/0 can be remotely compromised. Both the patching and the security group configuration are customer responsibilities in IaaS.
Pro-Tip
Use immutable image pipelines for VM builds and enforce patch baselines via automation to reduce human error and drift.
Common Mistake

Assuming network security is fully handled by the CSP. Security groups and NACLs are configured by you and are a frequent source of exposure.

screens.title: Customer responsibilities in PaaS
screens.narratorSegment: Platform as a Service reduces some operational burdens by shifting runtime, OS, and middleware maintenance to the provider. That means you no longer worry about server patching or runtime availability, but you must still secure the application, its data, and how identities access the platform. Core customer tasks include secure coding practices, application vulnerability scanning, database access rules and encryption of stored data, managing A P I keys and environment variables securely, and configuring platform-specific security settings like network access and role assignments. A common oversight in PaaS is treating the platform as a guarantee that application logic is safe. In reality, the provider keeps the platform patched but will not fix vulnerabilities in your code, nor enforce least privilege inside your application. For example, a managed database is patched by the CSP, but user roles, sensitive column encryption, and credentials are your responsibility. Operationalize PaaS security with secure deployment pipelines, secrets management, runtime monitoring, and platform configuration reviews. Misconception check: PaaS reduces infrastructure chores but increases the need for strong application governance. Customer responsibilities in PaaS means shift away from os maintenance toward application, data, and platform configuration security; enforce secure development and secrets handling.. In practical terms, how responsibility shifts when the provider manages runtimes and middleware. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › PaaS Responsibilities
Process

Where the boundary moves in PaaS

Provider covers
Runtime patching, middleware maintenance, and underlying infrastructure availability.
Customer covers
  • Application code and dependencies
  • Data encryption and classification
  • Secrets and API key management
  • Platform configuration and access controls
Key Takeaway

PaaS reduces host management but increases application governance responsibilities; treat platform settings and secrets as first-class security objects.

Concrete Example
A managed database is patched by the CSP, but you must create strong database users, limit privileges, and encrypt sensitive columns. Platform maintenance does not remove your need for least-privilege design.
Misconception
Believing that PaaS automatically protects application-level vulnerabilities is incorrect; use SAST and DAST in your pipelines and protect runtime secrets.

screens.title: Customer responsibilities in SaaS
screens.narratorSegment: In Software as a Service the provider manages nearly the entire stack: infrastructure, platform, and application. That greatly reduces your operational burden but does not remove customer responsibilities. Key duties that remain with the customer include identity and access management for user accounts, multi-factor authentication, data classification and governance, secure configuration of sharing and privacy settings, and retention or deletion policies. For instance, moving email and productivity to a SaaS provider means the vendor handles uptime, OS patching, and application updates, but you must enforce MFA, assign roles carefully, and configure data retention to meet compliance needs. A common pitfall is granting overly broad permissions within the SaaS application or ignoring account lifecycle controls. The practical strategy is to centralize identity where possible, enforce strong authentication, review application-level roles periodically, and ensure you have export and retention controls for regulated data. Misconception check: SaaS does not remove the need for governance — it shifts it toward people, identities, and data policies. Customer responsibilities in SaaS means providers run the app stack; customers own identity controls, data governance, and application configurations.. In practical terms, when the provider manages the whole application stack. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › SaaS Responsibilities
Comparison

What stays with you in SaaS

Identity and access
User accounts, MFA, role assignments, and lifecycle management remain customer duties.
Data governance
Classification, retention policies, export controls, and compliance mapping stay with the customer.
Application configuration
Privacy settings, sharing options, and permission scopes must be configured and audited by you.
Key Takeaway

SaaS reduces platform risk but increases reliance on identity hygiene and data governance — prioritize those controls.

Concrete Example
A SaaS office suite operator manages the service's availability and patching. You must enable MFA for users, set sharing defaults to private, and implement retention rules to satisfy compliance.
Misconception
Believing SaaS removes organizational responsibility for data lifecycle or access is a risky assumption that leads to exposed data and weak audit trails.

screens.title: How responsibilities shift: IaaS → PaaS → SaaS
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing the three service models clarifies where controls move as you adopt higher-level services. In IaaS you are responsible for the operating system, middleware, runtime, applications, and data; the provider secures the physical hosts, virtualization layer, and global network. Moving to PaaS, the provider takes on runtime and middleware, leaving you to secure the application code, data, and platform configuration. In SaaS the provider manages the entire application stack, leaving you primarily responsible for identity, data governance, and per-tenant application settings. This shift impacts tooling and process choices: security automation for IaaS needs system patching and endpoint hardening; PaaS requires strong CI/CD checks for code quality and secret management; SaaS requires identity federation, role reviews, and data retention policies. A common mistake is reusing the same control set for different models — for example, expecting OS patching automation to cover a SaaS offering. Instead, map controls to the model: network controls and host patching for IaaS, secure development and secrets management for PaaS, and identity governance for SaaS. This clear mapping lets you prioritize controls where responsibility lies. How responsibilities shift: IaaS → PaaS → SaaS means as you move from iaas to saas, provider responsibilities increase while customer duties narrow toward identity and data governance.. In practical terms, a side-by-side view of who owns what. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › IaaS / PaaS / SaaS Comparison
Comparison
IaaS
  • Customer: OS, apps, network configs, data
  • Provider: physical hosts, hypervisor, core network
  • Tooling focus: patching, segmentation
PaaS
  • Customer: app code, data, secrets, platform settings
  • Provider: runtime, middleware, infra
  • Tooling focus: CI/CD security, secret rotation
SaaS
  • Customer: IAM, data governance, app config
  • Provider: full app stack, availability, patches
  • Tooling focus: identity federation, DLP, retention
Key Takeaway

Assign controls to the party responsible and choose tools that align with whether you need host-level patching, secure code checks, or identity governance.

Check Your Policy
When adopting a new service, list expected responsibilities and verify them against the CSP's shared responsibility matrix before deployment.

screens.title: Frequent pitfalls and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: Many cloud breaches stem from a small set of recurring mistakes. The most common include leaving storage buckets or containers publicly accessible, creating overly permissive network security rules, failing to patch virtual machines, mismanaging secrets and A P I keys, and granting excessive permissions to users and services. Each of these is a customer-side failure under the shared responsibility model. To avoid them, adopt guardrails: enable account-level public access blocks and automated configuration scanning to prevent public storage where it’s not intended; enforce security group templates and deny rules to avoid wide-open ports; implement continuous patching for hosts and container images; store secrets in managed secret stores rather than environment variables; and apply least-privilege IAM combined with periodic role reviews. A useful practical control is to add automatic alerting for new resources that deviate from hardened baselines. Misconception check: believing that a managed service automatically removes the need for runtime scans or secret rotation is risky. The recommended pattern is defense in depth — combine prevention, detection, and rapid remediation for customer-side responsibilities. Frequent pitfalls and how to avoid them means guardrails, automation, and least-privilege reduce human error and prevent common customer-side misconfigurations.. In practical terms, misconfigurations that lead to breaches and practical guards. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Common Misconceptions

Common missteps

These mistakes are frequent and preventable. They all represent customer-side responsibilities in the shared model.

Public storage
Misconfigured bucket policies or ACLs expose sensitive data. Use account-level blocks and scan for public objects.
Open network ports
Security groups allowing inbound access from anywhere enable remote compromise. Use restrictive rules and bastion hosts where needed.
Secrets in code

screens.title: Breach analysis: S3 bucket and EC2 compromise
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a real scenario from the chapter: an AWS IaaS deployment where a sensitive S3 bucket was publicly accessible and an EC2 instance ran an unpatched vulnerable web application. First, identify responsibilities: the public bucket policy and the EC2 OS patching are customer responsibilities — the CSP provides S3 and EC2 services but not your per-tenant policies or guest OS maintenance. AWS is responsible for the physical security and the service infrastructure. Second, propose mitigations for each customer-side failure. For the S3 bucket, apply an account-level public access block, fix the bucket policy, and add automated configuration checks. For the EC2 instance, enable automated patch management, scan for vulnerabilities, and use an image pipeline to redeploy hardened instances. For the vulnerable web application, integrate SAST/DAST into CI/CD and place a WAF in front of the application. Execute these mitigations together: prevent misconfigurations, detect drift, and contain incidents. Misconception check: blaming the CSP for an account-level policy or an unpatched guest OS misplaces responsibility. The clear takeaway is to map each failing control to whether it is a customer duty and then apply the correct remediation path.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Breach Analysis
Scenario

S3 bucket public + unpatched EC2

Assign responsibilities and propose concrete mitigations for the customer's failures.

Responsibility breakdown
  • S3 public access: Customer — bucket policy and ACL configuration
  • Unpatched EC2 OS: Customer — guest OS patching and image management
  • Underlying S3/EC2 physical infrastructure: CSP
Recommended mitigations
  • Apply account-level public access blocks and remediate bucket policies.
  • Automate patching for EC2 via a patch manager and use hardened AMIs.
  • Integrate SAST/DAST into pipelines and deploy a WAF in front of the app.
Command examples
aws s3api put-public-access-block \
  --bucket your-sensitive-data-bucket \
  --public-access-block-configuration "BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true"
aws ssm send-command \
  --instance-ids "i-0abcdef1234567890" \
  --document-name "AWS-RunPatchBaseline" \
  --comment "Apply OS patches" \
  --parameters 'Operation=Install'
Key Takeaway

Map each failing control to the customer or CSP and apply the correct remediation: account-level policy fixes and automation for customer duties.

screens.title: General customer responsibilities and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Across service models certain customer responsibilities persist and should be institutionalized. First, data classification: know what you store and label sensitivity to drive encryption and retention choices. Second, identity and access management: implement strong authentication, role-based access, and enforce least privilege across all cloud tenants. Third, auditing and logging: collect audit trails and monitor them for suspicious activity. Fourth, incident response: prepare a cloud-aware incident response plan that includes service-specific containment and recovery steps. Fifth, vendor due diligence: verify the CSP’s certifications and their shared responsibility documentation before trusting critical workloads. Operationalize these with automated checks and policies: CSPM tools to detect misconfigurations, SIEM for log aggregation, automated patching pipelines, and secrets management integrated into CI/CD. A common misconception is that inability to manage cloud-native logging or IAM means relinquishing responsibility; it does not. You must own these controls or add managed services and contractual evidence that the vendor meets your requirements. The ultimate takeaway: build repeatable, auditable processes for the customer-side responsibilities so they scale with cloud adoption. General customer responsibilities and best practices means data classification, iam, logging, incident response, and vendor due diligence remain customer priorities across all models.. In practical terms, operational controls every organization should implement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
Today we will make the shared responsibility model clear and usable. This model separates what the cloud provider secures from what you, the customer, must secure. The concise rule to remember is: the provider secures the cloud itself — the data centers, network fabric, and service infrastructure — while you secure everything you place into the cloud: your data, applications, identities, and configurations. Understanding this split prevents expensive gaps and common breaches. In practical terms, when you run an EC2 virtual machine or store files in a managed object store, the provider keeps the hardware and service running; you must patch the operating system, set access policies, and encrypt sensitive data. Throughout this lesson you will see concrete examples for IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS, learn common missteps like public buckets and open security groups, and get clear mitigations to apply in enterprise environments. By the end you should be able to explain responsibility boundaries to stakeholders and design controls that close customer-side gaps.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to clearly state which party is accountable for specific cloud security controls across IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS. You will learn to identify CSP responsibilities such as physical security and the security of managed services, and contrast them with customer duties like operating system patching, application hardening, network configuration, and identity management. You'll practice analyzing how responsibility boundaries shift with the service model and how those shifts affect control selection and monitoring. You'll also gain strategies to operationalize these responsibilities — for example, account-level controls to block public object access or automated patching for virtual machines — so you can design remediation plans. Finally, you'll learn to communicate these distinctions to stakeholders and avoid common misconceptions that lead teams to assume a provider handles configuration or access control when it does not. This competency helps prevent configuration gaps and strengthens cloud risk management.

This second objectives screen focuses on measurable skills and the assessments you can use to confirm them. You will practice mapping responsibilities in a breach scenario, proposing mitigations for customer-side failures, and using provider documentation to verify responsibility boundaries. One concrete task will ask you to analyze an AWS IaaS breach involving an open S3 bucket and an unpatched EC2 instance, identify which parts were the customer's responsibility, and list specific mitigations such as account-level public access blocks, automated patching, and Web Application Firewalls. The ability to produce a short remediation plan and to justify each control based on the shared responsibility model is the key competency here. You will also learn to spot common misconceptions — for example, assuming a provider automatically enforces host-level hardening — and to translate findings into prioritized actions for security teams.

We begin by defining the two central terms you will use constantly: security of the cloud and security in the cloud. Security of the cloud is the provider's duty to secure the infrastructure that runs services: physical data centers, network fabric, hypervisors, and the internal code that implements managed services. Providers maintain physical access controls, redundant networking, and patching at the service layer so you can rely on a hardened foundation. Security in the cloud is everything you are accountable for when using cloud services: your data, applications, operating systems you deploy, configuration of network controls, and identity management. For example, a CSP will protect the servers that host object storage, but you are responsible for the bucket policies and object ACLs that govern who can read your data. A useful misconception check: never assume a provider configures your service endpoints, access rules, or encryption keys for you by default. The takeaway is a working claim: the CSP secures the environment; you secure your usage of it. To practice, name one service you use and list which parts the provider controls and which parts you must harden. That exercise will reveal hidden responsibilities.

In an Infrastructure as a Service model you take on the largest share of security duties. The provider secures the physical hosts, virtualization layer, and the network fabric, but you are responsible for everything you install or configure on your virtual machines and services. That responsibility includes patching and hardening the operating system, managing host-based firewalls and anti-malware, securing application code, managing security groups and network ACLs, encrypting data at rest and in transit, and implementing identity and access controls with least privilege. A common breach pattern is an unpatched virtual machine combined with an overly permissive security group allowing SSH from anywhere; both are customer failures that invite compromise. To operationalize IaaS security, use automated patch management, vulnerability scanning, baseline hardening templates, least-privilege IAM roles, and network segmentation. Also maintain logging and alerts so you can detect unauthorized access quickly. Misconception check: do not assume that because the provider manages the network hardware, your virtual network configuration is secure by default. The immediate takeaway is: treat each VM and storage resource as your operational responsibility and bake patching and configuration as repeatable automation.

Platform as a Service reduces some operational burdens by shifting runtime, OS, and middleware maintenance to the provider. That means you no longer worry about server patching or runtime availability, but you must still secure the application, its data, and how identities access the platform. Core customer tasks include secure coding practices, application vulnerability scanning, database access rules and encryption of stored data, managing A P I keys and environment variables securely, and configuring platform-specific security settings like network access and role assignments. A common oversight in PaaS is treating the platform as a guarantee that application logic is safe. In reality, the provider keeps the platform patched but will not fix vulnerabilities in your code, nor enforce least privilege inside your application. For example, a managed database is patched by the CSP, but user roles, sensitive column encryption, and credentials are your responsibility. Operationalize PaaS security with secure deployment pipelines, secrets management, runtime monitoring, and platform configuration reviews. Misconception check: PaaS reduces infrastructure chores but increases the need for strong application governance. Customer responsibilities in PaaS means shift away from os maintenance toward application, data, and platform configuration security; enforce secure development and secrets handling.. In practical terms, how responsibility shifts when the provider manages runtimes and middleware. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

In Software as a Service the provider manages nearly the entire stack: infrastructure, platform, and application. That greatly reduces your operational burden but does not remove customer responsibilities. Key duties that remain with the customer include identity and access management for user accounts, multi-factor authentication, data classification and governance, secure configuration of sharing and privacy settings, and retention or deletion policies. For instance, moving email and productivity to a SaaS provider means the vendor handles uptime, OS patching, and application updates, but you must enforce MFA, assign roles carefully, and configure data retention to meet compliance needs. A common pitfall is granting overly broad permissions within the SaaS application or ignoring account lifecycle controls. The practical strategy is to centralize identity where possible, enforce strong authentication, review application-level roles periodically, and ensure you have export and retention controls for regulated data. Misconception check: SaaS does not remove the need for governance — it shifts it toward people, identities, and data policies. Customer responsibilities in SaaS means providers run the app stack; customers own identity controls, data governance, and application configurations.. In practical terms, when the provider manages the whole application stack. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Comparing the three service models clarifies where controls move as you adopt higher-level services. In IaaS you are responsible for the operating system, middleware, runtime, applications, and data; the provider secures the physical hosts, virtualization layer, and global network. Moving to PaaS, the provider takes on runtime and middleware, leaving you to secure the application code, data, and platform configuration. In SaaS the provider manages the entire application stack, leaving you primarily responsible for identity, data governance, and per-tenant application settings. This shift impacts tooling and process choices: security automation for IaaS needs system patching and endpoint hardening; PaaS requires strong CI/CD checks for code quality and secret management; SaaS requires identity federation, role reviews, and data retention policies. A common mistake is reusing the same control set for different models — for example, expecting OS patching automation to cover a SaaS offering. Instead, map controls to the model: network controls and host patching for IaaS, secure development and secrets management for PaaS, and identity governance for SaaS. This clear mapping lets you prioritize controls where responsibility lies. How responsibilities shift: IaaS → PaaS → SaaS means as you move from iaas to saas, provider responsibilities increase while customer duties narrow toward identity and data governance.. In practical terms, a side-by-side view of who owns what. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Each of these is a customer-side failure under the shared responsibility model.
